opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a great question, because becoming a manager really changed how I think about communication.

As an engineer or a researcher, you can get away with being a little vague, because a lot of the work happens in your own head. You know what you mean, the code compiles, and that's enough. Once you're leading a team, that stops working. Whatever is in your head doesn't automatically end up in other people's heads. I learned that the hard way. I'd say something I thought was perfectly clear, and a week later someone would come back with something quite different from what I had in mind. It wasn't their fault. My message just wasn't as clear as I thought it was.

So a few things changed for me.

First, I try to explain the *why*, not just the *what*. If people understand the goal and the reasoning, they can make good decisions without me, and often better ones than I would have. If I only give instructions, I become the bottleneck.

Second, I write things down a lot more. Writing forces you to be precise. If I can't write a clear one-page explanation of what we're trying to do, that usually means I haven't thought it through yet. So writing helps me think, not just communicate.

Third, I check for understanding. Instead of asking "Is that clear?", which everyone answers with yes, I'll ask someone to describe how they plan to approach it. That catches misunderstandings early, when they're cheap to fix.

And finally, I've learned that clear communication goes both ways. As a manager, a big part of the job is listening and making it safe for people to say "I don't understand" or "I think this plan is wrong." If people don't feel comfortable saying that, you lose a lot of information, and you end up making decisions based on a picture of reality that isn't accurate.

So I'd say being a manager taught me that communication isn't a soft skill on the side. It's really the core of getting anything meaningful done with other people.

r001.rationale: The response says to check understanding by asking someone to describe their planned approach, which reveals misunderstandings early.

r002.rationale: It describes messages being understood differently than intended, but does not say that speaking at length can leave the listener receiving little.

r003.rationale: It calls listening a big part of a manager’s job, but does not identify listening as more important than speaking a lot.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, becoming a manager was the first time I realized how bad I was at communicating. When I was mostly writing code, say in the early days of Taichi, I could get away with being vague because the only person who had to understand me was me, or maybe one or two collaborators who shared all my context. Once I was running a team, every unclear sentence I said turned into hours of wasted work for someone else. That's a very expensive feedback loop, and it teaches you fast.

The biggest lesson is that clarity is mostly about reducing the receiver's workload, not about sounding precise. Engineers love to be technically correct, but a message that's technically correct and takes ten minutes to parse is still a bad message. So now I try to lead with the conclusion, then the reasoning, then the details. If someone only reads the first line, they should still know what I want and why.

The second thing is that silence is information too. When I say something and nobody pushes back, early on I assumed that meant agreement. It usually meant people didn't understand, or didn't feel safe saying they disagreed. So I started explicitly asking people to repeat back what they think the plan is. It feels a bit awkward at first, but the gap between what I said and what they heard was often shocking.

And the last part is writing things down. Verbal communication is lossy, and as a company grows you simply can't be in every room. A good design doc or a clear written decision scales in a way that my voice doesn't. So I'd say managing made me a much more disciplined writer, and that discipline fed back into how I think about problems in general.

r001.rationale: The speaker says they explicitly ask people to repeat back the plan to reveal gaps between what was said and understood.

r002.rationale: The response discusses unclear messages and misunderstandings, but does not say that speaking at length can leave listeners receiving very little.

r003.rationale: The response describes checking for understanding, but does not identify listening as more important than speaking a lot.

astra-6.text:
Being a manager has made me realize that saying something clearly and having it understood are two different things. You might have a very clear picture in your head, but the other person doesn’t necessarily have the same context. So you have to explain not only what you want to achieve, but also why it matters and what the constraints are.

I think communication is also a feedback loop. Instead of just asking, “Does that make sense?” it helps to ask, “How would you approach this?” Their answer tells you whether you actually share the same understanding. If you don’t, that’s a signal to revisit your explanation. That has made me more conscious of the assumptions I bring into a conversation.

r001.rationale: The response describes communication as a feedback loop and using the listener’s answer to check whether they share the same understanding, then revisiting the explanation if needed.

r002.rationale: It does not say that speaking extensively can still leave the listener receiving little of the message.

r003.rationale: It mentions eliciting feedback but does not identify listening as more important than speaking a lot in managerial communication.

sol-6.1.text:
Being a manager has made me realize that communication isn’t just about saying something clearly in my own mind. It’s about whether the other person walks away with the same understanding. You can explain a goal, everyone can nod, and then discover a week later that people had very different interpretations.

So I try to make the context explicit: what we’re trying to achieve, why it matters, and what the constraints are. Then I ask questions and give people room to explain their understanding. That feedback is really important. If there’s a misunderstanding, I need to look at how I communicated, rather than simply assuming someone wasn’t listening.

r001.rationale: The response says the manager asks questions and gives people room to explain their understanding, using that feedback to catch misunderstandings.

r002.rationale: It describes people interpreting an explanation differently, but does not say that speaking at length can still result in the listener receiving very little.

r003.rationale: It describes asking questions and hearing feedback, but does not identify listening as more important than speaking a lot.
